lesson.title: Beyond Concavity: Meet the Third Derivative
lesson.summary: The third derivative tells you how concavity itself is changing, and you find it by differentiating a function three times in a row.
lesson.body:
Once you've learned that the second derivative f''(x) measures concavity, that is, how the slope f'(x) is changing, a natural question follows: does that concavity change smoothly, or does it shift abruptly? Answering that requires differentiating one more time. The third derivative is simply what you get when you take the derivative of the second derivative, continuing the same process you already know.

Formally, the third derivative of f is f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)]. It is the derivative of a derivative of a derivative: differentiate f once to get f', differentiate f' to get f'', then differentiate f'' one more time to get f'''. Nothing new is required mechanically, you use the same differentiation rules (power rule, product rule, chain rule, and so on) at each step; the only change is which function you are differentiating at each stage.

You will see the third derivative written a few different ways: f'''(x) using three prime marks, y''' if the function is named y, or f^(3)(x) using a parenthesized superscript. That last form becomes important once you get past three derivatives, since writing five or six prime marks in a row gets unreadable fast; f^(3)(x) means exactly the same thing as f'''(x).

Let f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2. Differentiate once: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 6x. Differentiate again: f''(x) = 12x^2 - 6. Differentiate a third time: f'''(x) = 24x. So the third derivative is the linear function 24x. You can evaluate it anywhere: f'''(1) = 24(1) = 24, and f'''(-2) = 24(-2) = -48. Each of these numbers describes how fast the concavity of the original curve is changing at that particular x-value.

Third derivatives are not just an algebra exercise. When a function describes the position of a moving object over time, its third derivative has a specific physical name, jerk, which you'll meet a little later in this unit. For now, the key habit to build is comfort with repeated differentiation: each derivative is just doing the same operation again, applied to whatever function came out of the previous step.
